T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Hands-on-keyboard intrusion by pbeesly on scranton (Invoke-Discovery/Persistence/ScreenCapture/Exfil, Add-Type VirtualAlloc loader, PsExec64 with plaintext password to NASHUA) included full-access LSASS handle opens on scranton and nashua.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: NASHUA: wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass with 0x1f3fff and the PsExec-delivered C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe sessions repeatedly queried the LSA registry key, then harvested and archived credential-named files.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: Only lsass.exe internal writes to HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F and LogonUI LoggedOnSAMUser; no reg save/hive export, no SAM file creation, no 4663/4656 SAM access.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: All NTDS checks (command lines, .dit file creation, 4663 ntds objects, other/powershell text) returned zero hits.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: Only two 4662 SecretObject reads of Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC by NT AUTHORITY\LOCAL SERVICE on utica; no Policy\Secrets registry modification or lsadump tooling.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: lsass.exe wrote HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 four times on nashua and once on scranton, coinciding with the PsExec logons as pbeesly — cache population caused by the intrusion, no cachedump tooling or non-lsass access to the Cache key.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No 4929 events, no drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync references, and no DS-Replication access on the utica domain object.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture behaviour observed is the Azure Network Watcher guest extension on scranton.dmevals.local: netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes' / 'trace stop' spawned by NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (Microsoft CoreXT, Networking-NetAnalytics) which was installed by WindowsAzureGuestAgent via enable.cmd, loading only the Microsoft-signed hnetmon.dll; the accompanying logman ETW traces are children of WaAppAgent.exe. No pktmon/dumpcap/windump/RawCap/Wireshark/Npcap or wpcap/npf driver load was found (C058, C059 zero hits), and the actual intrusion in the window (PsExec64 with plaintext credentials launching an unsigned C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua) used no sniffing tooling.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Parent technique: LSASS credential access by PowerShell on scranton (0x1FFFFF handle + CreateRemoteThread into lsass) and by wsmprovhost on nashua (0x1f3fff) constitute input/credential capture activity.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger indicators: keyboard registry writes are OS layout/device keys; zero hits for keylog/GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx in command lines, image loads or script blocks; no keylogger service installed.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Only legitimate consent.exe UAC prompts and PowerShell credential-object construction; no fake credential GUI or input-box harvesting.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No writes to wwwroot/inetpub or login pages, no 4663 access on web roots; Zeek HTTP shows only WebDAV file transfer (exfil), not portal capture.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass with 0x1FFFFF/0x1f3fff (UNKNOWN call trace) and created a remote thread in lsass with an unbacked start address; wsmprovhost.exe on nashua also opened lsass with 0x1f3fff.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: No 4625 failed logons anywhere in windows.security, no failed-logon messages in windows.other, and no login/brute-force tooling in sysmon process creation. The password-related hits are the attacker's own hardcoded credentials in PowerShell scripts, not password attacks.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: Zero 4625 events and no guessing tooling; the only keyword hit was a hidden PowerShell bitmap-decoding stager whose command line merely contains '-ep bypass'.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: Credential material was harvested rather than cracked: pbeesly's powershell.exe opened lsass with 0x1fffff on scranton (03:05:16Z), wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua (03:09:29Z), and lsass requested SAM_SERVER handles with 0xf003f on scranton (03:19:21Z, 03:20:46Z). No hashcat/john, ntds.dit or hive file writes were seen, so the offline cracking step is absent.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No failed logons to form a spray pattern. The repeated pbeesly network logons (Kerberos type-3 from 10.0.1.4 and PSEXESVC 4648 explicit-credential logons on nashua) are reuse of one already-compromised account for lateral movement, not spraying across many accounts.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: The only 'credential'/'password' script hits are Microsoft localization strings and the attacker's single hardcoded exfil credentials ('cozy'/'MyCozyPassw0rd!'); no stolen credential lists were replayed against logon services.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran a Get-PrivateKeys PowerShell function that enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported every certificate with its private key to password-protected .pfx files (confirmed artifact C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx), then opened lsass.exe with full access (0x1fffff), staged the loot into OfficeSupplies.7z and copied it to a WebDAV share, and finally deleted the .pfx files. This is theft of certificate-based authentication material used for MFA/smart-card logon. The 4648 DWM/UMFD/SCRANTON$ events and the CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManager registry writes were benign OS activity.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: SCRANTON (10.0.1.4) as pbeesly ran Invoke-Exfil PowerShell that maps \\192.168.0.4\webdav via New-PSDrive and copies OfficeSupplies.7z there; sysmon shows powershell.exe and svchost.exe (WebClient) connecting to 192.168.0.4:80, and zeek shows Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt OPTIONS/PROPFIND to /webdav answered 401 after SMB 445/139 to the same host was rejected — WebDAV-based forced authentication. NASHUA's python.exe also beacons to 192.168.0.4:8443 against a self-signed cert.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's hidden, execution-policy-bypassed PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) that had loaded VirtualAlloc/CreateThread shellcode opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff and an UNKNOWN() call-trace frame at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, alongside private-key (.pfx) theft and exfil staging — exploitation of LSASS for credential access. Other LSASS handle access (svchost/lsm.dll, wininit, csrss, Azure telemetry, wsmprovhost Get-Process) is benign OS/PowerShell-remoting behaviour.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No browser cookie store was read, copied or exfiltrated. Cookie/credential-store filename matches were Edge's own runtime files created by MicrosoftEdge.exe on scranton and a svchost.exe write to the LocalService INetCookies package path; no 4663 object access to Cookies/Login Data/Web Data, and no process command line or script block referencing cookies, sqlite or a browser credential database (the 4104 keyword hits were Microsoft module manifests loaded by SYSTEM on newyork). The malicious activity present on scranton (Draft.Zip document/password-file collection, screen capture, 7-Zip + WebDAV exfil to \\192.168.0.4\webdav) is file/input collection and exfiltration, not web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credential material was harvested on scranton.dmevals.local: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported every LocalMachine certificate's private key to .pfx files in the user's Downloads folder, which the same session then compressed and staged for exfiltration.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: NASHUA: PowerShell under python.exe enumerated *pass*/*psw*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn/*.pst/*.ost files in the user profile and compressed them into working.zip, then Rar.exe password-protected it and sdelete64.exe wiped the artifacts.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All registry writes to password/credential paths are OS activity (CredentialGuard, CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, IdentityCRL, Winlogon PasswordExpiryNotification); no reg query/save, cmdkey or vaultcmd execution and no 4663 access to credential registry keys.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No reference to ConsoleHost_history, Get-History or any history file in script blocks, process command lines, file creations or object accesses; the only .txt-referencing process is the Azure guest agent's logman.exe.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: SCRANTON: Get-PrivateKeys exported every LocalMachine certificate with private key to Downloads\<random>.pfx with password 'saribas'; the .pfx files were then 7-Zip'd into OfficeSupplies.7z and deleted.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SCRANTON: PowerShell read HKLM\SOFTWARE\Javasoft 'value Supplement' and Invoke-Expression'd it, spawning a base64 hidden PowerShell after an elevated hostui.exe launch.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Hidden steganographic PowerShell PID 2976 on scranton (spawned via sdclt/control from a malicious .scr) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff and an UNKNOWN call trace at 03:05:16Z, corroborated by Security 4656 AccessMask 0x1fffff for user pbeesly.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: SCRANTON: sdclt.exe UAC-bypass launches by cmd.exe immediately preceded hidden steganographic PowerShell and csc.exe compiles; no browser credential-store file read was observed.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: Vault/Credential Manager artifacts (vaultcli.dll, vaultsvc.dll, deletion of Microsoft\Vault\UserProfileRoaming\Latest.dat by lsass.exe) on scranton shortly after the LSASS dump access, but no vaultcmd/cmdkey execution or object-access events to confirm theft.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden execution, .kdbx files or password-manager process access; Rar.exe on nashua is staging, not password-manager theft.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Hidden steganographic PowerShell (monkey.png decode, PID 2976, DMEVALS\pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16, inside a broader SeaDuke/PsExec intrusion.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: No DC authentication patching: no lsass/cryptdll service install, no Lsa/SecurityProviders/WDigest registry change, no 4739; LSASS access on DCs is AV/telemetry/system with read-only masks.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No DLL written to System32/SysWOW64 and no Notification Packages / PasswordFilter registry modification.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No ReversibleEncryption/Set-ADAccountControl/dsmod usage in PowerShell or process command lines and no 4739 events.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739 policy change and no MFA-related configuration events; logon types/processes are ordinary.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory-service changes and no anomalous DLLs loaded into cloud-identity processes.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider registry write (Sysmon 13 or 4657); np/provider image loads are standard Windows components.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No interception evidence: Sysmon connections go to DCs/telemetry endpoints; the single NTLM network logon (pbeesly on scranton from 172.18.39.2) matches the DC's own DNS forwarder address used by newyork dns.exe.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: Only six NBT name queries to 10.0.1.255 with no responses and no LLMNR/5355 traffic; SMB records are routine IPC$/sysvol GPO reads from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4; no poisoning/relay tooling or script blocks.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: arp.exe /a and route.exe print are read-only Azure guest-agent/telemetry calls on scranton; no arpspoof/poison script blocks; Zeek shows one stable responder MAC (12:34:56:78:9a:bc) for the DC, not duplicated/spoofed L2 addresses.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP events exist in windows.other (no 1341/1342/1020/1063) and Zeek has no dhcp log type, so rogue DHCP cannot be assessed; the only network-config commands (netsh trace, ipconfig /all) are Azure agent diagnostics.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: A real intrusion chain is present (cod.3aka3.scr → cmd/powershell on scranton, SeaDuke PowerShell toolkit, Invoke-SeaDukeStage to NASHUA, PSEXESVC spawning C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua) and LSASS handle-access events exist, but no Kerberos ticket theft or forgery was observed; the rare LSASS accesses map to system components and managed PowerShell call traces.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: krbtgt 4769 requests are normal pbeesly logons (AES256, Status 0x0) and all 4768 events show PreAuthType 2; no forged-ticket or KRBTGT-dumping indicators.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service tickets are only for machine accounts NEWYORK$/NASHUA$ with AES256 and success status; no anomalous service-account elevation or forged service-ticket logons.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No burst of TGS requests for user SPNs, no RC4 service tickets, and zero PowerShell hits for kerberoast/SPN/GetUserSPNs tooling.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 14 TGT requests used pre-authentication (PreAuthType 2) and no asrep/GetNPUsers tooling was found in sysmon or PowerShell logs.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential material (cookie or SAML) was created or used in the window; however credential-access precursor LSASS memory access by PowerShell (0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua, plus a malicious .scr and obfuscated PowerShell as pbeesly, were observed and are reported as suspicious.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Cookie/Login Data file writes were only svchost lastalive/GroupPolicy files and one MicrosoftEdge profile temp file; the only cookie/session PowerShell hit was a Get-AttributesMask helper. No forged cookie use.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/ADFS/token-signing script blocks; 4648 explicit-credential events are routine pbeesly/PSEXESVC and system-account logons.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 5 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly) enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported every certificate with private key to password-protected .pfx files in Downloads (coyn5igj.3io.pfx observed created by powershell.exe), followed by a cleanup script deleting Downloads\*.pfx — clear certificate/private-key theft for authentication.

findings.title: Full-access LSASS handle opened by PowerShell on scranton and by wsmprovhost on nashua during an active intrusion
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and then 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) — the classic LSASS memory-read mask used by credential dumpers. The call trace is ntdll/KERNELBASE followed by UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D), i.e. code not backed by a loaded module, consistent with injected/reflective code. This occurred inside a hands-on-keyboard intrusion by user pbeesly on scranton (same session ran Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Keystroke-Check, Invoke-Exfil and a VirtualAlloc/CreateThread Add-Type loader). Four minutes later, at 03:09:29, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, SYSTEM) on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1f3fff, immediately after pbeesly ran 'Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA { Get-Process -IncludeUserName ... }' and 'Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA' from scranton. The remaining LSASS accesses in the dataset are benign: svchost.exe with 0x1000 (query-limited), Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe/WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400, and csrss/wininit with 0x1fffff at boot.

evidence.value: Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA -ScriptBlock { Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Select-Object UserName,SessionId | Where-Object { $_.UserName -like "*\$env:USERNAME" } | Sort-Object SessionId -Unique } | Select-Object UserName,SessionId

findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, pbeesly used PsExec64.exe from scranton (10.0.1.4) with the cleartext password '-p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by' to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe four times (03:11:39-03:15:03). At 03:09:29 a wsmprovhost.exe WinRM session had already opened lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff (full access incl. read/write process memory). The python.exe sessions then repeatedly opened the LSA registry key (\REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa, AccessMask 0x1, Query key value) at 03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49 and 03:15:03, spawned powershell.exe, and beaconed to 192.168.0.4:8443. The PowerShell session enumerated files matching *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn*, *.pst, *.ost, compressed them to $env:APPDATA\working.zip, archived with Rar.exe -hpfGzq5yKw, then wiped Rar.exe and both zips with sdelete64.exe. This is new LSASS/credential-store access on nashua beyond the anchors (which only covered the wsmprovhost handle).
findings.title: NASHUA: python.exe delivered via PsExec opened LSASS with 0x1f3fff, then read LSA secrets and staged/exfiltrated a credential archive
PowerShell opened LSASS with full-access mask and created a remote thread in lsass.exe on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff, with a CallTrace ending in an UNKNOWN module (C:\windows\SYSTEM32\ntdll.dll+9c584|C:\windows\System32\KERNELBASE.dll+2732e|UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D)) — the classic signature of a credential-dumping tool calling OpenProcess on LSASS. In the same second Sysmon event 8 recorded a CreateRemoteThread from that same PowerShell process (PID 2976) into lsass.exe (PID 736), NewThreadId 912, StartAddress 0x00000117610E0000 with StartModule '-' (unbacked memory). Windows Security 4656 corroborates the handle request by C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff / 0x1f3fff. This is attacker activity consistent with API hooking / in-memory credential theft against LSASS, not normal system behaviour. (The second CreateRemoteThread into lsass at 03:18:34 came from csrss.exe with StartModule KERNELBASE.dll / StartFunction CtrlRoutine, which is a benign Windows mechanism.)

findings.title: Credential material harvested from lsass memory and SAM on SCRANTON by pbeesly's PowerShell, and from lsass on NASHUA via WinRM — offline cracking not observed
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16Z the process C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe running as pbeesly (logon 0x372e81) requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff (including 'Read from process memory'), and at 03:09:29Z wsmprovhost.exe as pbeesly opened lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local. On scranton, lsass.exe itself then requested SAM_SERVER handles with AccessMask 0xf003f at 03:19:21Z and 03:20:46Z. This is credential dumping from LSASS/SAM (the T1110.002 check family), but no hashcat/john/cracking tooling, no ntds.dit or hive file writes, and no 4663 reads of SAM/SECURITY were observed — the cracking step itself is not present in the data.

findings.title: No password spraying: no failed logons, and the repeated pbeesly network logons are lateral movement with already-stolen credentials
findings.summary: There are zero 4625 events, so no spray pattern exists. The 218 successful type-3 logons are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25, WEC$ 8, UTICA$ 5) plus 20 for pbeesly. The pbeesly logons are a single account reused across hosts — Kerberos type-3 from 10.0.1.4 to newyork and nashua, and explicit-credential 4648 events on nashua.dmevals.local from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe using pbeesly's credentials (03:11:40Z onward), following the Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA script on scranton at 03:10:22Z. findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no artifact of web-credential forging: no SAML/ADFS/token-signing or cookie/AES script blocks (C313, C324 zero hits), no browser cookie/Login Data file writes by anything other than svchost/MicrosoftEdge (C315/C316), and 4624 logon process/package stacks are ordinary (Kerberos 217, Advapi 76, User32 2, NtLmSsp 1). What is present is credential-access precursor activity: on scranton.dmevals.local PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16Z, and on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, PowerShell remoting host) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29Z. The scranton host also ran a malicious screen-saver C:\ProgramData\victim\...cod.3aka3.scr from explorer.exe as pbeesly at 02:55:56Z, later deleted with sdelete64.exe, and at 03:21:29Z pbeesly executed obfuscated PowerShell (GetProcAddress/ReflectedDelegate dynamic delegate + base64 PE blob, and a gzip+base64 scriptblock) - consistent with in-memory tooling that could harvest credentials. No forged cookie or SAML token was observed being created or used, so T1606 itself is not evidenced.

findings.title: Single ROOT certificate store blob modification on nashua by Sysmon.exe (no corroborating forgery activity)

It is the only SystemCertificates-related 4657 in the whole dataset (count 1), so it is not a routine pattern, but the writing process is Sysmon.exe and no certificate creation/export, forged-certificate use, or anomalous Kerberos ticket encryption was observed on nashua (all 14 4768 events use 0x12). Treated as suspicious-but-unconfirmed rather than confirmed forgery.

findings.title: SAM hive written by lsass.exe on scranton (normal SAM account-update behaviour, not a dump)

No reg save / hive export command line, no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive file creation (only Prefetch .pf files matched), and no 4663/4656 access to SAM or SECURITY hive objects were observed. Note: the intrusion on scranton did not need SAM dumping because the operator already had the plaintext password for dmevals\pbeesly, which was passed to PsExec64.exe on the command line.

findings.title: No NTDS.dit access, VSS copy or ntdsutil activity observed

findings.title: No DCSync: no directory-replication access on the DC and no drsuapi/lsadump tooling

findings.title: netsh packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is the Azure Network Watcher guest extension, not adversary sniffing
findings.summary: The only packet-capture activity in the Windows telemetry is on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z: netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (LogonId 0x3e7, IntegrityLevel System) with 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' and stopped ~7s later with 'netsh trace stop'. The agent binary reports Company 'Microsoft CoreXT' and Description 'Networking-NetAnalytics release_14_nwa (af53be328) Microsoft CoreXT'. The netsh process loaded only the Microsoft-signed hnetmon.dll (Signature 'Microsoft Windows', SignatureStatus Valid). The same NetworkWatcherAgent appears on nashua, scranton and utica (73 sysmon events, mostly registry), i.e. it is a fleet-wide Azure platform extension. The parallel logman.exe ETW trace create/start/stop commands (GAEvents, RTEvents, WindowsAzure-GuestAgent-Diagnostic writing to C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\*.etl) are likewise all children of C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\WaAppAgent.exe. Separately, the genuine intrusion in this window (pbeesly using PsExec64.exe with the plaintext password to run an unsigned C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua) shows no capture tooling, so T1040 is not part of the attacker's tradecraft here.

findings.title: No keylogger artefacts: keyboard registry writes and hook/image loads are OS baseline

No Sysmon 1 command line, Sysmon 7 image load, or PowerShell 4104 script block referencing keylog/GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx was found (checks C069, C070, C073 returned zero hits). No keylogger service was installed: the only 7045 service installs are javamtsup.exe and PSEXESVC.exe. Note that the malicious PowerShell on scranton (Invoke-Exfil, hidden -e encoded command, IEX from a bitmap) is credential/exfil activity, not input capture.

findings.title: Only genuine Windows consent.exe prompts; no fake credential GUI

findings.summary: No Sysmon registry write to a NetworkProvider key and no 4657 change to a NetworkProvider object were returned; the 4657 ObjectName values are WMI Autologger GUIDs and certificate/WSMAN keys. The 'np/provider' image-load hits are ordinary Windows components (npmproxy.dll, InputHost.dll, TextInputFramework.dll, facecredentialprovider.dll). The malicious PowerShell LSASS access is covered under T1556, not a network-provider implant.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; network and logon evidence consistent with normal domain operations
findings.summary: Across the Windows and Zeek windows there is no evidence of traffic interception. Sysmon EventCode=3 destinations are dominated by the domain controllers (192.168.0.4, 10.0.0.4) and local/loopback addresses, with the remainder being Microsoft/Office telemetry endpoints. The only NTLM network logon (4624, LogonType 3, NtLmSsp, NTLM V2) is pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:20:41-04:00 from 172.18.39.2 with Workstation Name 10.0.1.4; 172.18.39.2 is the address newyork.dmevals.local's dns.exe forwards queries to (source.ip 10.0.0.4, source.port 53), i.e. the DC's own DNS forwarder path, not a relay. The real attacker activity in this window is lateral movement (PsExec service installs by pbeesly on nashua.dmevals.local followed by C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe), which is outside the T1557 family.

findings.title: NBT-NS name queries and SMB sessions are routine domain traffic, not poisoning or relay
findings.summary: The only LLMNR/NBT-NS-port traffic is six NBT name queries (qtype NB, port 137) to the broadcast address 10.0.1.255: three from 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) at 2020-04-30T00:34:51-53Z and three from 10.0.1.4 (SCRANTON) at 00:35:01-03Z, with no responses captured and no LLMNR (5355) traffic at all. SMB file/mapping records come only from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4 (NEWYORK.dmevals.local) and are ordinary IPC$ and sysvol GPO reads (gpt.ini, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf). No relay tooling, no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning script blocks (PowerShell search returned zero hits), and the 4697 service installs are PsExec (PSEXESVC) and normal svchost-based services, not relay tooling.

findings.title: ARP/route enumeration is Azure guest-agent telemetry; no ARP cache poisoning indicators
findings.summary: The only arp.exe and route.exe executions are on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:24-03:20:04Z, run as SYSTEM by WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe and WaAppAgent.exe with the read-only arguments "arp.exe" /a and "route.exe" print — Azure VM health/telemetry collection, not ARP manipulation. No arpspoof/ARP-poison script blocks were found in PowerShell (zero hits). In the Zeek window the responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is used consistently for the domain controller 10.0.0.4 across DNS, SMB, Kerberos, LDAP, NTP and dce_rpc flows from both 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6, i.e. a single stable gateway/DC MAC rather than a duplicated or spoofed L2 address.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing: no DHCP events in any dataset, and network-config commands are Azure agent activity
findings.summary: DHCP client/server events (1341, 1342, 1020, 1063) are absent from windows.other, and the Zeek dataset contains no dhcp log type at all, so rogue DHCP offers/ACKs are not present in the collected data. The only DHCP/network-configuration command lines are on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17-03:19:57Z: netsh.exe trace start/stop spawned by NetworkWatcherAgent.exe and "ipconfig.exe" /all spawned by WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe and WaAppAgent.exe — Azure platform diagnostics, not DHCP manipulation. No dhcp/rogue script blocks in PowerShell (zero hits).

findings.title: No golden-ticket indicators: krbtgt TGS requests are normal pbeesly logons with pre-auth
findings.summary: windows.security contains 4768 (14) and 4769 (28) events, all on newyork.dmevals.local for pbeesly from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 with Status 0x0 and TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256). The krbtgt service-ticket requests carry TicketOptions 0x40810010/0x60810010 and the 4768 events all show PreAuthType 2, i.e. normal pre-authenticated TGT issuance. No 4769 for krbtgt with anomalous options, no RC4 downgrade, and no LSASS access by a dumping tool that would yield KRBTGT material. The high-access LSASS events (0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) come from csrss.exe, wininit.exe, PowerShell.exe and wsmprovhost.exe with managed-code call traces, not from a credential-theft utility.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators: service tickets are only for host accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$) by pbeesly
findings.summary: All 28 4769 events are on newyork.dmevals.local, requested by pbeesly (and SCRANTON$) for machine service accounts NEWYORK$ and NASHUA$ with AES256 (0x12) and Status 0x0; no service-account SPN tickets for user accounts, no RC4 (0x17) tickets, and no 4672 events attributable to a service account being elevated (the 4672 events are NEWYORK$ machine-account privilege assignments). The 4624 logon-type distribution (3:218, 5:61, 2:15, 10:2, 0:1) shows no unusual service-ticket-driven logon burst. The pbeesly network logons to nashua (LogonType 3, Kerberos) and the PSEXESVC LogonType 2 logons are lateral movement by the compromised account, not forged service tickets.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no burst of TGS requests for user SPNs and no roasting tooling
findings.summary: Only 11 TGS requests appear in zeek (2020-04-30 window, non-overlapping with the Windows data) and 28 4769 events in windows.security, all for machine accounts NEWYORK$/NASHUA$ with AES256 encryption and success status — no single account requesting many distinct service SPNs, no RC4-encrypted service tickets typical of Kerberoasting. PowerShell script-block searches for kerberoast/SPN/Invoke-Kerberoast/GetUserSPNs returned zero hits; the observed PowerShell content is SeaDuke-style discovery/persistence/screen-capture/exfil code, not ticket extraction.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: all 14 TGT requests used pre-authentication
findings.summary: All 14 4768 events on newyork.dmevals.local have win.PreAuthType 2 (pre-authentication enabled) with Status 0x0, so no account requested a TGT without pre-auth. No AS-REP roasting tooling was found: the sysmon process-creation search for asrep/GetNPUsers/kerberos command lines and the PowerShell script-block search for asrep/AS-REP/GetNPUsers/preauth both returned zero hits.

findings.title: No browser cookie theft or forged-cookie use observed
findings.summary: The cookie-related checks produced only benign results. File-creation events matching *Cookies*/*Login Data*/*Web Data* (162 events) are dominated by svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceState\EventLog\Data\lastalive0.dat / lastalive1.dat (133+28) and GroupPolicy DataStore files, plus a single MicrosoftEdge.exe write of C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Packages\Microsoft.MicrosoftEdge_8wekyb3d8bbwe\AC\MicrosoftEdge\User\Default\DataStore\_TempTestAccess.txt - normal Edge profile behaviour, not cookie exfiltration. The only PowerShell script block matching cookie/session keywords was a Get-AttributesMask helper function (token/privilege enumeration code), not cookie manipulation. No forged cookie was observed being injected or replayed.

findings.title: No SAML token forging activity (no ADFS/token-signing artifacts)
findings.summary: Searches for SAML/ADFS/token-signing script blocks returned zero hits, and the 4648 explicit-credential events (15 total) are ordinary: pbeesly explicit logons from 10.0.1.6 on scranton and via PSEXESVC on nashua, plus DWM/UMFD/winlogon/taskhostw system account logons. No SAML token was observed being forged or replayed in this window.

findings.title: Remaining 4657 registry writes are WMI Autologger/WSMAN configuration, not certificate tampering
findings.summary: Of the 36 Security 4657 events, 34 target \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\WMI\Autologger\EventLog-Application\{GUID} values (Enabled/MatchAnyKeyword) written by C:\Windows\System32\wevtutil.exe under SCRANTON$ on scranton.dmevals.local at 23:19:16, and one targets \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WSMAN\SafeClientList. These are event-log autologger and WSMAN configuration changes, not certificate store or CA configuration, so they do not support certificate theft/forgery. Kerberos TGT requests (14 x 4768) all used encryption type 0x12 with no anomalous pattern.

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access mask by PowerShell on scranton (and wsmprovhost on nashua)
incidents.rationale: All describe the same LSASS handle-open events: PowerShell PID 2976 on scranton with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and UNKNOWN call trace, plus wsmprovhost.exe on nashua with 0x1f3fff. F23/F32/F36 add the steganographic loader context for the same PID 2976 event; F52 notes the same precursor with no web-credential forging. Best fit: OS Credential Dumping - LSASS Memory.

incidents.title: NASHUA: python.exe via PsExec opened LSASS, read LSA secrets, staged credential archive
incidents.rationale: LSASS 0x1f3fff access plus LSA registry reads and credential archive staging on nashua. Best fit LSASS Memory.

incidents.title: Cached domain credential registry writes by lsass (benign logon caching)
incidents.rationale: NL$1 writes by lsass align with PsExec logons; assessed as caching, not cachedump. Best-fit technique is Cached Domain Credentials.

incidents.title: Credential material harvested from LSASS/SAM; no offline cracking observed
incidents.rationale: Describes LSASS and SAM handle access as credential harvesting; the technique assigned is Password Cracking per the finding, though cracking itself was not observed.

incidents.title: No password spraying; reused pbeesly credentials for lateral movement
incidents.rationale: Finding explicitly rules out spraying and attributes repeated logons to lateral movement with stolen credentials; technique retained as assigned.

incidents.title: WebDAV/UNC forced authentication to attacker server 192.168.0.4 from scranton
incidents.rationale: New-PSDrive to \\192.168.0.4\webdav with explicit credentials and DavClnt/401 WebDAV artifacts; forced authentication.

incidents.title: NASHUA python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443 with self-signed TLS
incidents.rationale: Same external endpoint as the forced-auth WebDAV activity; assessed as credential-capture listener interaction. Best fit Forced Authentication.

incidents.title: Credential-harvesting tooling staged as .ps1 in SysinternalsSuite; no plaintext credential files read
incidents.rationale: Attacker scripts masquerading as Sysinternals content; no credential files read. Best fit Credentials In Files.

incidents.title: NASHUA: harvested password/login-named files into working.zip
incidents.rationale: Recursive enumeration of credential-bearing file patterns and archiving. Best fit Credentials In Files.

incidents.title: SCRANTON: unsigned .scr dropper launched by explorer.exe writing monkey.png payload
incidents.rationale: Initial dropper for credential-access tooling; technique retained as Credentials In Files per finding, though the action is execution/delivery.

incidents.title: SCRANTON: accesschk.exe permission reconnaissance from staged SysinternalsSuite
incidents.rationale: Permission reconnaissance supporting credential access; technique retained as Credentials In Files per finding.

incidents.title: Certificate/private-key export via Get-PrivateKeys to .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: Same Get-PrivateKeys script block (readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and Export-PfxCertificate to Downloads with password 'saribas'. Private key material theft.

incidents.title: SCRANTON: registry value read and Invoke-Expression'd, hostui.exe elevated
incidents.rationale: Registry value read and executed; no plaintext credential observed. Technique retained as Group Policy Preferences per finding.

incidents.title: SCRANTON: sdclt.exe UAC-bypass launcher followed by hidden steganographic PowerShell
incidents.rationale: Elevation/loader activity; no browser credential store read observed. Technique retained as Credentials from Web Browsers per finding, though unconfirmed.

incidents.title: Windows Vault / Credential Manager artifacts touched on scranton
incidents.rationale: vaultcli/vaultsvc loads and Vault Latest.dat deletion by lsass; low confidence, no vaultcmd usage. Best fit Windows Credential Manager.

incidents.title: Compromised host chain scranton→nashua with LSASS access; no Kerberos ticket theft observed
incidents.rationale: SeaDuke toolkit and LSASS access but no ticket theft/forgery; technique retained as Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets per finding.

incidents.title: Certificate harvesting followed by archive and exfiltration (scranton)
incidents.rationale: F19 covers the Get-PrivateKeys export plus Invoke-Exfil archiving and exfiltration; the credential-access action is stealing authentication certificates. F56 is separate (see below).

incidents.title: ROOT certificate store blob modification on nashua by Sysmon.exe
incidents.rationale: Single 4657 modification of a SystemCertificates ROOT blob; certificate-store tampering, low confidence, no corroborating forgery.
